name: Flutamide topical (melasma)

lead: Flutamide is an antiandrogen pill used for prostate cancer. A 1% topical version has been tried off-label for melasma, the facial pigmentation disorder, as an alternative to hydroquinone, to even out facial skin tone.

It blocks androgen receptors; the sources reviewed do not explain how this would affect melasma pigmentation. Wikipedia's melasma article cites a randomized trial comparing topical 1% flutamide with hydroquinone, but does not report its results.

paras: The topical use is a compounded cream applied to melasma patches, studied against hydroquinone. Flutamide itself is a prescription drug.
The oral drug carries a warning for severe liver injury and is prescription-only. No data on systemic absorption or safety of the topical form were found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: An oral prostate-cancer antiandrogen studied off-label as a 1% topical for melasma, to even out facial pigmentation by blocking androgen receptors locally. One randomized comparison with hydroquinone is cited.

lead: Flutamide is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen taken by mouth, used mainly for prostate cancer. It blocks androgen receptors [1]. A 1% topical preparation has been studied as an alternative treatment for melasma, a pigmentation disorder of the face [2].

Wikipedia's melasma article cites a randomized trial that compared topical 1% flutamide with hydroquinone but does not report its results or safety profile [2]. The oral drug carries a warning for severe liver injury [1]; the sources reviewed contain no data on systemic absorption or safety of the topical form.

paras: Oral flutamide's main use is prostate cancer, often together with GnRH analogues. It has also been used in women for acne, seborrhea, hirsutism, scalp hair loss and hyperandrogenism, though liver risk limits this and it is no longer recommended as a first- or second-line option [1].
For melasma, 1% topical flutamide is listed among alternatives to the standard topical depigmenting agents such as hydroquinone, tretinoin, azelaic acid, kojic acid and arbutin [2].

Oral flutamide has caused severe liver injury and deaths, and its risk is described as higher than that of bicalutamide or nilutamide. Liver function monitoring is advised during oral treatment. It is listed as pregnancy category D [1]. Whether these risks apply to topical use is not addressed in the sources reviewed.
A randomized trial comparing 1% topical flutamide with hydroquinone in melasma is cited on Wikipedia, which does not report its outcomes [2]. No other studies were reviewed here.

timeline.event: Flutamide first synthesized as a bacteriostatic agent; antiandrogen activity discovered later [1].
Flutamide approved in the United States [1].
